paper.citation: Oliva-Lozano JM, Gómez-Carmona CD, Rojas-Valverde D, Fortes V, Pino-Ortega J. Effect of training day, match, and length of the microcycle on the worst-case scenarios in professional soccer players. Research in Sports Medicine. 2021.
paper.abstract: Cohort study of 23 professional soccer players from one LaLiga 123 team across 56 sessions (43 training sessions and 13 official matches) in the 2018-2019 season. Worst-case scenarios (WCS) for distance, high-speed running distance and sprint distance over 1, 3, 5 and 10 minutes were calculated from GPS data and compared by session type and microcycle length.
paper.tldr: In professional soccer, match days produced the highest worst-case scenario demands, and training sessions 3 to 4 days before a match came closest to match peaks but still fell short. The length of the microcycle changed training-day demands but had little effect on match-day demands.
paper.methods: Cohort design across four in-season mesocycles, with WIMU Pro GPS units sampling at 10 Hz and rolling-average WCS calculated for distance (above 0 km/h), high-speed running (above 19.8 km/h) and sprint distance (above 25.2 km/h). A mixed ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests compared session days and 5-6, 7 and 8 day microcycles, and goalkeepers were excluded.
paper.findings: Match-day WCS were higher than training-day WCS at every intensity and duration, with effect sizes from moderate (distance over 1 and 3 minutes) to high (all other measures). Among training days, the highest WCS for all three measures occurred at MD-4, MD-3 and MD+1, and the lowest at MD-2 and MD-1. Microcycle length significantly affected training-day WCS but had no significant effect on match-day WCS.
paper.limitations: Data came from a single professional team, and environmental conditions, match location, formation and playing position were not analysed. Speed thresholds were not individualised, and GPS has known satellite-related accuracy limits. The authors caution against generalising beyond this context.
paper.practicalImplications: Staff could consider 1 to 10 minute high-intensity drills 3 to 4 days before matches to rehearse match worst-case periods, because training WCS were highest on those days but still below match demands. Training-day load should be planned with the length of the microcycle in mind. The authors flag a possible overtraining risk from repeated high-intensity training, which was not tested.
paper.athleteDev: Performance and conditioning staff can use rolling-average worst-case scenarios to see which training days come closest to match peaks. Match-day peaks were consistent across microcycle lengths, while training-day demands varied with microcycle length.
paper.rtp: The study measured in-season training and match demands in squad players and did not assess injured players or rehabilitation, so it cannot be used to guide return to sport decisions.
